strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing an important gap in visual prompt tuning interpretability, particularly relevant for safety-critical applications
Novel application of category-agnostic hierarchical concept prototypes to visual prompt tuning, enabling shared concepts across categories
Comprehensive quantitative evaluation with multiple baselines, architectures (DeiT, DinoV2), and consistent improvements (5-8% on consistency scores)
Coherent technical framework combining CRD, IFA, and fine-to-coarse fusion with thoughtful design choices like consistency loss for cross-layer alignment
Diverse applications demonstrated on fine-grained classification, pathology images (Gleason-2019), and car recognition, showing generalizability
Ablation studies validating each component's contribution and clear presentation with effective visualizations of the approach
weaknesses: Interpretability evaluation relies almost entirely on one metric (consistency scores) on a single dataset (CUB-200-2011 with keypoint annotations); other datasets evaluated only qualitatively without quantitative interpretability metrics
No human evaluation or user studies to validate that learned concepts are truly 'human-understandable' despite this being a central claim
Missing computational cost analysis—no evaluation of training time, memory, or inference overhead compared to baseline VPT, critical for parameter-efficient methods
Lack of statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing; improvements (5-8%) reported from single runs without validation

Incremental technical novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (part-shaping losses from [1], Gumbel-Softmax grouping, standard attention mechanisms); main novelty is application to visual prompt tuning
Performance degrades on smaller models (DinoV2-S lags Huang et al. by 2.2%), suggesting limited scalability and raising questions about method's practical applicability
Hyperparameter choices appear arbitrary (17, 14, 11, 8 prototypes; 4 fused prompts) with no sensitivity analysis or justification
Weak baselines: 'VPT (w/ Proto.)' variants artificially apply prototypes only at last layer, not genuine competing methods
Reproducibility concerns: part-shaping loss details relegated to prior work [1], no code release mentioned, supplementary material referenced but not provided
Limited scope: evaluation restricted to fine-grained classification; effectiveness on coarse-grained tasks or other modalities unknown
Missing failure case analysis and no systematic evaluation of what concepts are learned; visualizations appear cherry-picked

strengths: Addresses an important problem of interpretability in visual prompt tuning, which is timely and relevant.
Comprehensive evaluation on CUB-200-2011 across multiple architectures with detailed comparisons to both part-prototype and VPT baselines.
Intuitive hierarchical structure design for capturing multi-granularity concepts across transformer layers.
Ablation studies (Table 2) demonstrate meaningful contributions from each component, particularly +5% consistency gain from hierarchical structure.
Demonstrates applicability across domains: fine-grained classification, medical imaging, and car recognition through qualitative results.
Well-motivated combination of concept-based and attribution-based interpretability approaches.
Clean presentation of the overall framework with helpful visualizations of concept regions and importance scores.
weaknesses: Critical evaluation gap: Quantitative results only on CUB-200-2011; Gleason-2019 and Stanford Cars are presented as main applications but lack any quantitative metrics (accuracy, consistency, stability). This undermines claims of comprehensive evaluation.

No human evaluation studies validating interpretability despite it being the core contribution. Consistency/stability metrics only measure alignment with provided annotations, not true interpretability to human users.
Marginal accuracy improvements (~0.5-0.7% over baselines) do not justify the added architectural complexity (multiple loss terms, hierarchical structure, fusion layers, additional modules).

Limited technical novelty: CRD uses standard negative Euclidean distance + Softmax from cited work; IFA is simple feature averaging; Gumbel-Softmax grouping and fusion are standard techniques. Main contribution is packaging existing methods in the VPT context.

Category-agnostic claim unsubstantiated: No direct comparison between category-specific and category-agnostic prototypes; prototypes inherently reflect training data distribution regardless of category-agnostic design.

Critical design choices lack justification: (1) Why exactly 17-14-11-8 prototypes? (2) Why equal loss weights in Eq. 14? (3) Why does forcing fine-to-coarse region alignment improve interpretability? No ablations or sensitivity analyses provided.

Reproducibility concerns: Part-shaping loss Lps details omitted from main paper; hyperparameters in appendix; no computational cost analysis; no code availability mentioned; missing optimizer details, learning rates, batch sizes.
Inconsistent performance: IVPT lags Huang et al. [18] on DinoV2-S consistency (63.5% vs 65.7%), with weak justification about 'limited capacity of smaller models.' Undermines robustness claims.
Analysis of failure cases absent: No discussion of when and why IVPT fails or underperforms baselines. Limited discussion of method limitations beyond brief mention in conclusion.

Evaluation metrics limitations: Single-run results without error bars or significance testing. CUB test set has only 5,794 images—results could be sensitive to noise. Metrics depend on provided annotations (circular validation).

Hierarchical structure justification incomplete: Figure 6 shows region maps but lacks quantitative evidence that coarse regions are more semantically meaningful. No comparison of interpretability quality at different granularities.
Missing key ablations: Sensitivity to prototype counts, loss weight ratios, concept region consistency loss impact, prototype initialization effects.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Addresses the underexplored challenge of interpretability in visual prompt tuning, which is important for safety-critical applications
Strong empirical results: Consistent improvements in consistency scores (+8.4% to +7.3% across models) and stability metrics compared to part-prototype networks
Elegant technical design: The combination of Concept Region Discovery, Intra-region Feature Aggregation, and hierarchical fusion is well-integrated and clearly presented

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Quantitative evaluation on 5 model variants, proper ablation studies (Table 2) showing each component's contribution, and qualitative analysis on diverse domains
Category-agnostic prototypes: Learning shared concepts across categories is more efficient and arguably more natural than category-specific approaches
Hierarchical organization with clear benefits: Multi-layer structure with fine-to-coarse alignment yields intuitive interpretation at multiple semantic granularities (+5% consistency improvement)
Broad applicability demonstrated: Evaluation on pathology and car classification shows applicability beyond fine-grained bird classification
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: Core techniques are largely adaptations of existing part-prototype methods (ProtoPNet, TesNet) and closely follow PDiscoFormer for region discovery; main contribution is their specific combination for prompt tuning
Single quantitative evaluation dataset: Only CUB-200-2011 used for quantitative metrics; Gleason2019 and Stanford Cars only show qualitative results, limiting the strength of empirical claims

Reliance on annotation-based evaluation: Consistency/stability metrics require keypoint annotations, making interpretability assessment difficult without such annotations and raising questions about true generalization

Underperformance on smaller models: Method lags behind Huang et al. [18] by 2.2% on DinoV2-S; explanation provided (limited model capacity) is unsatisfying and suggests potential generalization issues
Missing computational cost analysis: No discussion of overhead from hierarchical prototypes, additional losses, and region computation; training time and memory comparisons absent
Hyperparameter choices lack justification: Prototype numbers per layer (17, 14, 11, 8) and fused prompts (4) appear arbitrary with limited ablation; no sensitivity analysis provided
Loss function design not justified: All loss terms equally weighted (weight=1) in Eq. 14 without ablation or justification; equal weighting may not be optimal
Incomplete technical exposition: Why negative squared Euclidean distance? Spatial bias injection mechanism in Eq. 7 not explained; connection between grouping and loss could be clearer
No failure case analysis: Missing discussion of when/why the method fails; no analysis of images where interpretability breaks down; edge cases unexplored

Category-agnostic advantage not fully demonstrated: Claims about shared concepts not backed by analysis; missing visualization of prototype sharing patterns and direct comparison with category-specific interpretability

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: interpretability of visual prompt embeddings in VPT

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets (CUB, PartImageNet, PASCAL-Part), architectures (DeiT, DinoV2), with both quantitative metrics and human studies (97.5% annotation accuracy)
Well-motivated cross-layer hierarchical concept structure with intuitive fine-to-coarse semantic alignment, supported by high cross-layer IoU (98%+)
Systematic ablation studies (Tables 3-4) validating each component's contribution; includes analysis of generalization to unseen categories and domain shift
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and reproducible implementation details; code promised to be available
Demonstrates consistent improvements in consistency and stability metrics across multiple backbones and datasets
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core components (attention-based region discovery, feature aggregation, cross-layer fusion) adapt existing prototype-based techniques; mainly combines existing methods rather than proposing fundamentally new techniques

Interpretability evaluation relies on proxy metrics (consistency/stability scores) rather than direct measures of prompt interpretability; these metrics were designed for part-prototype networks, not prompt understanding

Missing comparisons with other interpretability approaches (attention visualization, gradient-based methods, TCAV) to justify that concept prototypes are superior for understanding prompts specifically
Inconsistent empirical performance undermines claims: IVPT achieves 63.5% consistency on DinoV2-S vs. 65.7% for Huang et al., contradicting superiority claims on some configurations
Category-agnostic prototype claim underjustified: no rigorous analysis of whether concepts actually transfer across categories or why this is better than class-specific prototypes

Computational overhead (4.8% training time, 5.2% inference latency) is non-negligible for a method targeting parameter efficiency; acknowledged limitation on in-domain dependency with no proposed solution

Limited generalization validation: experiments are primarily on fine-grained classification; CIFAR-100 and ImageNet results are qualitative visualizations without quantitative metrics or accuracy comparisons
Design choices lack rigorous justification (e.g., Gumbel-Softmax for grouping, KL divergence for region consistency, why mean aggregation in Eq. 9)
No statistical significance testing: results lack error bars, confidence intervals, or p-values despite claiming improvements

Human evaluation study (20 participants) focuses on concept annotation accuracy and transition naturalness but does not demonstrate whether understanding prototypes helps users understand what prompts actually do to model behavior

strengths: Addresses an important but underexplored problem: interpretability of visual prompt tuning, which is essential for trustworthy AI
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets, backbones, metrics, and includes human evaluation study (20 participants)
Well-designed system with thoughtful integration of concept discovery, region grounding, and cross-layer alignment components
Clear presentation with effective visualizations demonstrating learned concepts across different domains (birds, cars, aircraft, pathology)
Category-agnostic prototype design enables concept sharing across classes, which is a reasonable contribution
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily applies existing part-prototype learning techniques (ProtoPNet, PDiscoformer) to VPT; explicitly follows prior work's part-shaping loss functions; incremental contribution rather than fundamental innovation

Inconsistent quantitative results: underperforms Huang et al. (2023) on smaller models (DinoV2-S by 2.2%), and accuracy improvements over VPT baselines are marginal (<1%), raising questions about scalability and practical significance

Narrow evaluation scope: primary quantitative evaluation limited to fine-grained classification with explicit part annotations (CUB-200-2011); generalization to general datasets (ImageNet, CIFAR-100) only qualitative in appendix

Missing critical comparisons: recent interpretable prompt tuning methods (Bie et al. 2024, Yao et al. 2023, Prompt-CAM) are mentioned but not quantitatively compared; mainly compares against standard classification methods, not other interpretable adaptation approaches

Acknowledged severe limitations restricting applicability: requires in-domain prototypes, assumes clear part structure, fails on texture/scene understanding tasks; bad case analysis shows learning spurious correlations (bird legs on branches)

Methodological concerns: evaluates only 10 concepts from one layer despite learning concepts at multiple layers; uses spatial overlap (IoU) to validate cross-layer alignment rather than semantic alignment; unclear integration mechanism with actual VPT pipeline
Human study limitations: 97.5% concept annotation accuracy seems suspiciously high; no inter-rater agreement reported; small sample (20 participants); Likert scale ratings (4.7-4.8/5) are subjective

Incomplete ablations: does not isolate contribution of individual loss terms to interpretability vs accuracy trade-off; no sensitivity analysis for hyperparameters like number of layers/prototypes per dataset

Reproducibility issues: promised code URL not provided in manuscript; many design choices (17,14,11,8 prototypes per layer) appear dataset-specific with no principled selection procedure for new domains
Non-negligible computational overhead (4.8% training time, 5.2% inference latency) for a parameter-efficient method, yet underexplored in main paper

strengths: Addresses an important and largely unexplored problem: interpretability of visual prompt tuning, with clear motivation for safety-critical applications
Novel framework combining cross-layer concept prototypes with visual prompt tuning, featuring category-agnostic prototype sharing that enables generalization across categories

Comprehensive experimental evaluation including multiple datasets (CUB-200-2011, PartImageNet, PASCAL-Part, Gleason-2019, Stanford Cars, FGVC-Aircraft), multiple architectures (DeiT-S/B, DinoV2-S/B/L), extensive ablations, human evaluation (97.5% accuracy), and qualitative visualizations

Consistent empirical improvements: outperforms conventional prototype networks on consistency scores (+8.4% for DeiT-S), higher stability scores demonstrating robustness, maintains/improves classification accuracy
Well-designed hierarchical architecture with principled cross-layer fusion using concept region consistency loss (KL divergence in Eq. 8), effectively capturing fine-to-coarse semantic progression
Practical considerations transparently addressed: minimal computational overhead (0.12% of ViT-B parameters, 4.8% training time, 5.2% inference latency increase)
Strong qualitative analysis demonstrating cross-category concept generalization and intuitive hierarchical progression aligned with human visual reasoning
Clear presentation with effective figures and comprehensive appendix including additional ablations, human evaluation methodology, and failure case analysis
weaknesses: Individual technical components are incremental: CRD uses standard Euclidean distance with Softmax, IFA is simple feature averaging, part-shaping losses directly borrowed from Aniraj et al. (2024); novelty primarily lies in architectural integration rather than methodological innovation

Underperformance vs. Huang et al. (2023) on DinoV2-S (2.2% consistency gap) suggests scalability limitations to smaller models; explanation ('limited capacity') is speculative and warrants deeper analysis

Insufficient justification of design choices: prototype counts (17→14→11→8) appear arbitrary, fused prompt count (n=4) unjustified, loss weights (λ=1) treated uniformly without sensitivity analysis; hyperparameter sensitivity underexplored

Concept discovery mechanism unclear: paper doesn't explain why attention-based region discovery yields semantic concepts vs. random spatial patterns; prototype initialization sensitivity not explored despite random initialization scheme

Limited generalization evidence beyond fine-grained classification: CIFAR-100 and ImageNet results relegated to appendix with only qualitative visualizations; no quantitative metrics for general-domain classification

Evaluation metrics limitations: consistency/stability scores only computed on CUB-200-2011 (sole dataset with complete part annotations); PartImageNet and PASCAL-Part lack full quantitative evaluation; no statistical significance testing or error bars for main results

Category-agnostic prototype advantage underdeveloped: while claimed as key innovation, limited quantitative analysis isolating its specific benefit; ablation study doesn't clearly isolate category-sharing contribution from other design choices
Modest performance improvements in many cases (1-2% consistency score gains, e.g., 63.1 vs 61.3 for DinoV2-S), which while consistent, may not justify added complexity for practical applications
Failure modes (spurious correlations like bird prototypes on branches) acknowledged but not resolved; frequency and impact not quantified, limiting deployment confidence
Incomplete comparison with recent work: Prompt-CAM (Chowdhury et al., 2025) mentioned but not thoroughly compared; limited discussion of fundamental differences beyond prototype usage
Code availability incomplete (URL stated as 'available at' with no link provided), raising reproducibility concerns

Cross-layer alignment assumption (fine-grained regions should align with coarse-grained regions via Eq. 8) makes intuitive sense but alternative approaches unexplored; validation limited to IoU agreement rather than independent justification
